description_full: Sabre Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, operates as a software and technology company for the travel industry in the United States, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and internationally. It offers the Sabre Mosaic marketplace, a business-to-business travel marketplace that provides travel solutions for travel suppliers and buyers. The company also provides software technology products and solutions for airlines and other travel suppliers, including reservation systems for full-cost and low-cost carriers, commercial and operations products, agency solutions, and data-driven intelligence solutions. In addition, it offers SabreMosaic Airline Technology, an offer and order retailing platform for airlines. The company serves travel suppliers, such as airlines, hotels and other lodging providers, car rental brands, rail carriers, cruise lines, tour operators, attractions and services; a network of travel buyers, including online and offline travel agencies, travel management companies, and corporate travel departments; and airports, governments and tourism boards. Sabre Corporation was founded in 1960 and is headquartered in Southlake, Texas.

financial_summary: Sabre Corporation is a small-cap technology business with a $680M market cap on $2.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years and -1% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 2% against a 12% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.
The company is burning through $192M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
Accruals are elevated at +14.1% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 8.9× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 0.5× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 16% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
